tutorials.description: Creating Docker images for test frameworks, Docker Compose for test environments, container orchestration, and best practices.

content.title: The Case for Containerized Tests
content.explanation:
Docker revolutionizes API testing by providing consistent, reproducible environments. What runs on your laptop runs exactly the same way in CI and production.

**The Environment Consistency Problem**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ENVIRONMENT CONSISTENCY                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  Developer Laptop                                                │
│  ├── Python 3.9.5                                                │
│  ├── Node 16.14.0                                                │
│  ├── PostgreSQL 14                                                │
│  └── Custom config                                               │
│        │                                                          │
│        ▼                                                          │
│  CI Server                                                       │
│  ├── Python 3.9.7  ❌ Different patch                            │
│  ├── Node 18.12.0 ❌ Different major                             │
│  ├── MySQL 8.0    ❌ Different database                          │
│  └── Default config ❌ Different settings                        │
│        │                                                          │
│        ▼                                                          │
│  ❌ "Works on my machine" failures                               │
│                                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Docker Solution: Containerized Tests**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    CONTAINERIZED TESTS                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  Docker Image (Single Source of Truth)                           │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ FROM python:3.11-slim                                       │ │
│  │ RUN pip install -r requirements.txt                         │ │
│  │ COPY tests/ /tests                                          │ │
│  │ CMD ["pytest", "tests/"]                                   │ │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│        │                              │                         │
│        ▼                              ▼                         │
│  Developer Laptop                CI Server                       │
│  ┌────────────────┐             ┌────────────────┐              │
│  │ docker run     │             │ docker run     │              │
│  │ test-image     │             │ test-image     │              │
│  └────────────────┘             └────────────────┘              │
│        │                              │                         │
│        └──────────────┬───────────────┘                         │
│                       ▼                                          │
│              ✅ Same environment everywhere                      │
│              ✅ "Works everywhere"                              │
│                                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Benefits for API Testing**

| Benefit | Description | Impact |
|---------|-------------|--------|
| **Reproducibility** | Same environment everywhere | Eliminates "works on my machine" |
| **Isolation** | Tests don't interfere with host | No dependency conflicts |
| **Parallelism** | Run multiple test suites concurrently | Faster execution |
| **Dependency Management** | All dependencies in Dockerfile | No manual setup |
| **Version Control** | Dockerfile in git | Track environment changes |
| **CI/CD Integration** | First-class support in all CI tools | Seamless automation |
| **Scaling** | Easy to run on any infrastructure | Cloud, on-prem, hybrid |

**Docker in CI/CD Pipeline**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    DOCKER IN CI/CD PIPELINE                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  Commit → Build Test Image → Run Tests → Publish Results         │
│     │            │               │              │                │
│     ▼            ▼               ▼              ▼                │
│  git push    docker build    docker run     artifacts            │
│              test.Dockerfile  test-image                         │
│                                                                   │
│  # Example pipeline steps                                         │
│  docker build -t api-tests -f Dockerfile.test .                  │
│  docker run --rm api-tests                                       │
│  docker run --rm -e API_URL=$STAGING_URL api-tests               │
│                                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Key Insight:** Docker transforms API testing from a fragile, environment-dependent activity into a reliable, repeatable process. The initial investment in containerization pays dividends daily through eliminated setup issues and consistent results.

content.title: Dockerfile Best Practices for Test Images
content.explanation:
Creating efficient, secure, and fast test images requires following Docker best practices specifically tailored for testing.

**Basic Test Dockerfile**

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile.test
FROM python:3.11-slim AS base

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Set environment variables
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1

# Install system dependencies (minimal)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    curl \
    git \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Copy requirements first (for better caching)
COPY requirements.txt requirements-dev.txt ./

# Install Python dependencies
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt && \
    pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements-dev.txt

# Copy test code
COPY tests/ ./tests/
COPY src/ ./src/
COPY conftest.py pytest.ini ./

# Run tests by default
CMD ["pytest", "tests/", "-v", "--junitxml=reports/junit.xml"]
```

**Multi-Stage Build for Test Images**

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile.test
# Stage 1: Builder
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder

WORKDIR /build
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Test Runner
FROM python:3.11-slim

WORKDIR /app

# Copy Python packages from builder
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH

# Copy application code
COPY src/ ./src/
COPY tests/ ./tests/
COPY conftest.py pytest.ini ./

# Create non-root user
RUN useradd -m -u 1000 testuser && \
    chown -R testuser:testuser /app
USER testuser

CMD ["pytest", "tests/", "-v"]
```

**Language-Specific Test Images**

**Node.js Test Image**

```dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

FROM node:18-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# Copy node_modules from builder
COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules

# Copy test code
COPY . .

# Create non-root user
RUN addgroup -g 1000 -S testuser && \
    adduser -u 1000 -S testuser -G testuser
USER testuser

CMD ["npm", "test"]
```

**Java Test Image**

```dockerfile
FROM maven:3.8-openjdk-11 AS builder

WORKDIR /build
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline

FROM maven:3.8-openjdk-11

WORKDIR /app

# Copy dependencies from builder
COPY --from=builder /root/.m2 /root/.m2

# Copy source
COPY src ./src
COPY pom.xml .

# Run tests
CMD ["mvn", "clean", "test"]
```

**Optimizing Image Size**

```dockerfile
# Use slim variants
FROM python:3.11-slim  # 150MB vs 900MB
FROM node:18-alpine    # 170MB vs 1GB
FROM alpine:3.18       # 5MB base

# Clean package managers
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    package \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Use --no-cache for pip
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Multi-stage builds to exclude build tools
COPY --from=builder /app/dist /app

# Remove unnecessary files
RUN rm -rf /app/tests/__pycache__ /app/.git
```

**Dockerignore File**

```dockerignore
# .dockerignore
.git
.gitignore
.env
*.log
*.pyc
__pycache__/
.pytest_cache/
.coverage
htmlcov/
reports/
dist/
build/
*.egg-info/
.vscode/
.idea/
*.swp
*.swo
*~
Dockerfile
docker-compose*.yml
README.md
.gitlab-ci.yml
.github/
```

**Key Insight:** Well-optimized test images build faster, run faster, and are more secure. Multi-stage builds keep images small, `.dockerignore` prevents cache busting, and non-root users improve security. These practices make containerized tests practical for daily use.

content.title: Docker Compose for Test Environments
content.explanation:
Docker Compose orchestrates multi-container test environments, spinning up databases, message queues, and other dependencies alongside your test container.

**Basic Test Environment**

```yaml
# docker-compose.test.yml
version: '3.8'

services:
  # Test database
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: testuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpass
      POSTGRES_DB: testdb
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    tmpfs: /var/lib/postgresql/data  # Ephemeral storage
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U testuser"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
  
  # Redis for caching
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    tmpfs: /data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
  
  # Test runner
  test-runner:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.test
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://testuser:testpass@db:5432/testdb
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      API_URL: http://api:3000
    volumes:
      - ./reports:/app/reports  # Mount for test outputs
      - ./tests:/app/tests:ro    # Mount for live test updates
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock  # For Docker-in-Docker
```

**Complete API Test Stack**

```yaml
version: '3.8'

services:
  # API under test
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.api
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://appuser:apppass@db:5432/appdb
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      JWT_SECRET: test-secret
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:3000/health"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
  
  # Database
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: appuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: apppass
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb
    volumes:
      - ./init-db.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql
    tmpfs: /var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U appuser"]
      interval: 5s
  
  # Redis
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    tmpfs: /data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
  
  # Mock external services
  mock-payment:
    image: wiremock/wiremock:latest
    command: --port 8080 --verbose
    volumes:
      - ./mocks/payment:/home/wiremock
    ports:
      - "8081:8080"
  
  mock-email:
    image: mailhog/mailhog:latest
    ports:
      - "8025:8025"
      - "1025:1025"
  
  # Test runner
  test:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.test
    environment:
      API_URL: http://api:3000
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://appuser:apppass@db:5432/appdb
      PAYMENT_SERVICE_URL: http://mock-payment:8080
      EMAIL_SERVICE_URL: http://mock-email:1025
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
      mock-payment:
        condition: service_started
      mock-email:
        condition: service_started
    volumes:
      - ./reports:/app/reports
    command: ["pytest", "tests/", "-v", "--junitxml=reports/junit.xml"]
```

**Using Wait Scripts**

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# wait-for-services.sh

set -e

echo "Waiting for database..."
until pg_isready -h db -U testuser; do
  sleep 1
done

echo "Waiting for Redis..."
until redis-cli -h redis ping; do
  sleep 1
done

echo "Waiting for API..."
until curl -f http://api:3000/health; do
  sleep 1
done

echo "All services are ready!"
exec "$@"
```

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile.test with wait script
FROM python:3.11-slim

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    postgresql-client \
    redis-tools \
    curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

COPY wait-for-services.sh /usr/local/bin/
RUN chmod +x /usr/local/bin/wait-for-services.sh

# ... rest of Dockerfile

ENTRYPOINT ["wait-for-services.sh"]
CMD ["pytest", "tests/"]
```

**Running Tests with Docker Compose**

```bash
# Start test environment and run tests
docker-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml up --build --abort-on-container-exit

# Run with specific test
docker-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml run --rm test pytest tests/api/test_users.py

# Run in CI with exit code
docker-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml up --exit-code-from test

# Clean up
docker-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml down -v
```

**Key Insight:** Docker Compose creates production-like test environments with all dependencies. This catches integration issues that unit tests miss. The ephemeral nature (using `tmpfs`) ensures each test run starts with a clean slate, eliminating test pollution.

content.title: Docker in GitHub Actions
content.explanation:
GitHub Actions has first-class Docker support, making it easy to run containerized tests.

**Building and Running Test Container**

```yaml
name: Dockerized API Tests

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Build test image
        run: |
          docker build -f Dockerfile.test -t api-tests .
      
      - name: Run tests
        run: |
          docker run --rm \
            -e API_KEY=${{ secrets.API_KEY }} \
            -e API_URL=${{ secrets.API_URL }} \
            -v ${{ github.workspace }}/reports:/app/reports \
            api-tests
      
      - name: Upload test reports
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: test-reports
          path: reports/
```

**Using Docker Compose in GitHub Actions**

```yaml
name: Compose-based API Tests

on: [push]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2
      
      - name: Cache Docker layers
        uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-
      
      - name: Start test environment
        run: |
          docker-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml up -d db redis
          docker-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml build test-runner
      
      - name: Run tests
        run: |
          docker-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml run \
            -e API_KEY=${{ secrets.API_KEY }} \
            test-runner
      
      - name: Collect logs
        if: always()
        run: |
          docker-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml logs > docker-compose.logs
      
      - name: Upload artifacts
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: test-results
          path: |
            reports/
            docker-compose.logs
      
      - name: Clean up
        if: always()
        run: docker-compose -f docker-compose.test.yml down -v
```

**Multi-Architecture Testing**

```yaml
name: Multi-Architecture Tests

on: [push]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        platform: [linux/amd64, linux/arm64]
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Set up QEMU
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v2
      
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2
      
      - name: Build and test
        run: |
          docker buildx build \
            --platform ${{ matrix.platform }} \
            -f Dockerfile.test \
            -t api-tests \
            --load \
            .
          docker run --rm api-tests
```

**Key Insight:** GitHub Actions' Docker integration is seamless. Build once, run anywhere. The ability to cache layers dramatically speeds up subsequent runs, making containerized tests practical for CI.

content.title: Docker in GitLab CI
content.explanation:
GitLab CI has excellent Docker support, including Docker-in-Docker (DinD) for building and running containers.

**Basic Docker Job**

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages:
  - test

docker-tests:
  stage: test
  image: docker:24.0
  services:
    - docker:24.0-dind
  variables:
    DOCKER_DRIVER: overlay2
    DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: ""
  before_script:
    - docker info
    - docker version
  script:
    - docker build -f Dockerfile.test -t api-tests .
    - docker run --rm api-tests
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - reports/
```

**Docker Compose in GitLab CI**

```yaml
stages:
  - test

variables:
  DOCKER_DRIVER: overlay2
  DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: ""
  COMPOSE_FILE: docker-compose.test.yml

compose-tests:
  stage: test
  image: docker/compose:latest
  services:
    - docker:24.0-dind
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache docker-cli
    - docker version
    - docker-compose version
  script:
    # Start services in background
    - docker-compose up -d db redis
    # Build test image
    - docker-compose build test-runner
    # Run tests
    - docker-compose run test-runner
  after_script:
    - docker-compose logs > docker-compose.logs
    - docker-compose down -v
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - reports/
      - docker-compose.logs
    reports:
      junit: reports/junit.xml
```

**Using GitLab Container Registry**

```yaml
stages:
  - build-test-image
  - test

variables:
  TEST_IMAGE: $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE/test:latest

build-test-image:
  stage: build-test-image
  image: docker:24.0
  services:
    - docker:24.0-dind
  script:
    - docker login -u $CI_REGISTRY_USER -p $CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD $CI_REGISTRY
    - docker build -f Dockerfile.test -t $TEST_IMAGE .
    - docker push $TEST_IMAGE
  only:
    changes:
      - Dockerfile.test
      - requirements.txt

run-tests:
  stage: test
  image: $TEST_IMAGE
  script:
    - pytest tests/ -v --junitxml=reports/junit.xml
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: reports/junit.xml
  needs:
    - build-test-image
```

**Key Insight:** GitLab's Docker-in-Docker service makes container builds first-class citizens. The container registry integration means you can build test images once and reuse them across jobs, saving time and ensuring consistency.

content.title: Parallel Test Execution in Containers
content.explanation:
Run multiple test containers in parallel for faster execution, while managing shared resources carefully.

**Parallel Test Services**

```yaml
version: '3.8'

services:
  # Shared services
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: test
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test
    tmpfs: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    tmpfs: /data
  
  # Parallel test runners
  test-unit:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.test
    command: pytest tests/unit -v
    depends_on:
      - db
      - redis
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://test:test@db:5432/test
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
    volumes:
      - ./reports/unit:/app/reports
  
  test-api:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.test
    command: pytest tests/api -v
    depends_on:
      - db
      - redis
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://test:test@db:5432/test
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
    volumes:
      - ./reports/api:/app/reports
  
  test-integration:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.test
    command: pytest tests/integration -v
    depends_on:
      - db
      - redis
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://test:test@db:5432/test
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
    volumes:
      - ./reports/integration:/app/reports
```

**Running in CI with Parallel Jobs**

```yaml
# GitLab CI parallel test jobs
stages:
  - test

variables:
  COMPOSE_FILE: docker-compose.test.yml

before_script:
  - docker-compose up -d db redis

test-unit:
  stage: test
  script:
    - docker-compose run --rm test-unit
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - reports/unit/

test-api:
  stage: test
  script:
    - docker-compose run --rm test-api
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - reports/api/

test-integration:
  stage: test
  script:
    - docker-compose run --rm test-integration
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - reports/integration/

after_script:
  - docker-compose down -v
```

**Database Isolation for Parallel Tests**

```yaml
version: '3.8'

services:
  # Create separate databases for each parallel run
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_MULTIPLE_DATABASES: test_unit,test_api,test_integration
    volumes:
      - ./init-multiple-dbs.sh:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init-multiple-dbs.sh
    tmpfs: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  
  test-unit:
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:postgres@db:5432/test_unit
  
  test-api:
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:postgres@db:5432/test_api
```

**init-multiple-dbs.sh**

```bash
#!/bin/bash

set -e

# Create multiple databases
for db in test_unit test_api test_integration; do
  psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 --username "$POSTGRES_USER" <<-EOSQL
    CREATE DATABASE $db;
EOSQL
done
```

**Key Insight:** Parallel container execution dramatically speeds up test suites. The key is proper isolation—separate databases, unique ports, and independent test data—to prevent interference between parallel runs.

content.title: Test Data Management in Containers
content.explanation:
Managing test data in containerized environments requires strategies for initialization, isolation, and cleanup.

**Database Initialization**

```yaml
version: '3.8'

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: test
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test
      POSTGRES_DB: test
    volumes:
      # Initialize with schema
      - ./sql/schema.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/01-schema.sql
      # Load test data
      - ./sql/test-data.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/02-test-data.sql
      # Run migrations
      - ./sql/migrations:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/migrations
    tmpfs: /var/lib/postgresql/data
```

**Seed Data Script**

```sql
-- 01-schema.sql
CREATE TABLE users (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id),
    total DECIMAL(10,2),
    status VARCHAR(50)
);
```

```sql
-- 02-test-data.sql
INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES
    ('Test User 1', 'test1@example.com'),
    ('Test User 2', 'test2@example.com');

INSERT INTO orders (user_id, total, status) VALUES
    (1, 99.99, 'completed'),
    (1, 149.99, 'pending'),
    (2, 29.99, 'completed');
```

**Docker Volume for Persistent Test Data**

```yaml
version: '3.8'

volumes:
  test-data:
    driver: local

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    volumes:
      - test-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./init-db.sh:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init-db.sh
    tmpfs: /var/lib/postgresql/data  # Remove for persistence
```

**Dynamic Test Data Generation**

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile.test with data generator
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Install Faker for data generation
RUN pip install Faker

COPY generate_test_data.py /app/
COPY tests/ /app/tests/

# Generate fresh test data on each run
RUN python /app/generate_test_data.py --output /app/test-data.sql

CMD ["pytest", "tests/"]
```

**generate_test_data.py**

```python
from faker import Faker
import random

def generate_test_data(count=100):
    fake = Faker()
    with open('test-data.sql', 'w') as f:
        f.write("INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES\n")
        for i in range(count):
            name = fake.name()
            email = fake.email()
            comma = ',' if i < count - 1 else ';'
            f.write(f"    ('{name}', '{email}'){comma}\n")
```

**Key Insight:** Test data management is critical for reliable containerized tests. Use initialization scripts for schema, seed data for consistency, and generators for volume. Always clean up between runs to prevent test pollution.

content.title: Container Security Best Practices
content.explanation:
Running tests in containers requires attention to security, especially when handling credentials or running in CI/CD.

**Non-Root User**

```dockerfile
# Always create and use a non-root user
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Create user
RUN groupadd -r testuser && useradd -r -g testuser testuser

# Set ownership
WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=testuser:testuser . .

# Switch to non-root
USER testuser

CMD ["pytest"]
```

**Read-Only Root Filesystem**

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  test:
    build: .
    read_only: true  # Root filesystem read-only
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp
      - /app/reports  # Only directories that need write
    volumes:
      - ./reports:/app/reports  # Mount for output
```

**Secret Management**

```yaml
# docker-compose.test.yml
services:
  test:
    build: .
    environment:
      # DON'T: Hardcode secrets
      # API_KEY: sk_test_12345
      
      # DO: Use environment variables from host
      API_KEY: ${API_KEY}
      
      # DO: Use Docker secrets (Swarm mode)
      secrets:
        - api_key
      
      # DO: Use mounted secrets file
      volumes:
        - ./secrets/api-key.txt:/run/secrets/api-key:ro

secrets:
  api_key:
    file: ./secrets/api-key.txt
```

**Resource Limits**

```yaml
services:
  test:
    build: .
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: '2'
          memory: 2G
        reservations:
          cpus: '0.5'
          memory: 512M
    # Or for docker-compose run
    mem_limit: 2g
    cpu_shares: 1024
```

**Security Scanning**

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile.test with security scanning
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder

# Scan dependencies
RUN pip install safety && \
    safety check -r requirements.txt

# Scan filesystem
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y clamav && \
    freshclam && \
    clamscan -r /app
```

**CI Security Context**

```yaml
# GitHub Actions with security
name: Secure Container Tests

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Build with security
        run: |
          # Build with non-root user
          docker build -f Dockerfile.test -t api-tests .
          
          # Scan for vulnerabilities
          docker scout quickview api-tests
          docker scout cves api-tests
      
      - name: Run with read-only root
        run: |
          docker run --rm \
            --read-only \
            --tmpfs /tmp \
            -e API_KEY=${{ secrets.API_KEY }} \
            -v $PWD/reports:/app/reports \
            api-tests
```

**Key Insight:** Container security isn't optional—it's essential. Non-root users, read-only filesystems, resource limits, and secret management protect your infrastructure. Apply these practices even in development to build secure habits.

content.title: Kubernetes for Test Execution
content.explanation:
Kubernetes provides powerful orchestration for running containerized tests at scale, especially useful for performance testing and parallel execution.

**Test Job in Kubernetes**

```yaml
# test-job.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: api-test-job
spec:
  parallelism: 3  # Run 3 pods in parallel
  completions: 3  # Wait for 3 successful completions
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: test
        image: your-registry/api-tests:latest
        env:
        - name: API_URL
          value: "https://staging.example.com"
        - name: API_KEY
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-secret
              key: api-key
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
          limits:
            memory: "1Gi"
            cpu: "1"
        volumeMounts:
        - name: reports
          mountPath: /app/reports
      restartPolicy: Never
      volumes:
      - name: reports
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: reports-pvc
```

**Test Pod with Init Containers**

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-pod
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: init-db
    image: postgres:15
    command:
      - sh
      - -c
      - |
        until pg_isready -h postgres-service; do
          echo "Waiting for database..."
          sleep 2
        done
        echo "Database is ready"
  
  - name: migrate-db
    image: migrate/migrate
    command:
      - migrate
      - -path=/migrations
      - -database=postgres://user:pass@postgres-service:5432/testdb
      - up
    volumeMounts:
    - name: migrations
      mountPath: /migrations
  
  containers:
  - name: test
    image: your-registry/api-tests:latest
    env:
    - name: DATABASE_URL
      value: postgres://user:pass@postgres-service:5432/testdb
    volumeMounts:
    - name: reports
      mountPath: /app/reports
  
  restartPolicy: Never
```

**CronJob for Scheduled Tests**

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: nightly-api-tests
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"  # Daily at 2 AM
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: test
            image: your-registry/api-tests:nightly
            args: ["--performance", "--full-suite"]
            env:
            - name: ENVIRONMENT
              value: "production"
          restartPolicy: Never
```

**Key Insight:** Kubernetes orchestration shines for large-scale test execution. Use Jobs for parallel test runs, CronJobs for scheduled tests, and Init Containers for dependency management. This scales from dozens to thousands of test executions.

tutorials.title: Kubernetes for API Testing Environments
tutorials.description: K8s test environments, helm charts for test services, ephemeral environments, and testing in production-like clusters.

content.value:
Imagine being able to spin up a completely isolated, production-like environment for every single pull request, run your entire test suite, and then have it disappear automatically when you're done—all without waiting in queue or worrying about interfering with other developers' work. This is the promise of Kubernetes for API testing, and it's transforming how teams validate their software.

Traditional testing environments are often a source of friction. Shared staging environments create contention—teams fighting over who gets to deploy, tests failing because someone else changed the data, and long waits for availability. Local development environments rarely match production exactly, leading to the dreaded "it works on my machine" syndrome. Kubernetes solves these problems by giving every developer, every branch, every test run its own slice of infrastructure that behaves exactly like production.

content.title: The Testing Environment Challenge
content.explanation:
Before diving into Kubernetes solutions, it's important to understand the problems that make API testing difficult in traditional setups. These challenges compound as teams grow and systems become more complex.

**The Three Environments Problem**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ENVIRONMENT CHALLENGES                           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  🏠 Local Development                                            │
│  ├── Different operating systems (Mac vs Linux)                  │
│  ├── Different dependency versions                               │
│  ├── Limited resources (can't run full stack)                    │
│  ├── Network differences (firewalls, VPNs)                       │
│  └── Configuration drift (env vars, feature flags)               │
│                                                                   │
│  ☁️ Shared Staging                                               │
│  ├── Queue time: "Wait, is it my turn to deploy?"                │
│  ├── Test pollution: "Who changed the test data?"                │
│  ├── Flaky tests: "It passed locally but failed in staging"      │
│  ├── Resource contention: "The environment is slow today"        │
│  └── Configuration: "Staging doesn't match production"           │
│                                                                   │
│  🏭 Production                                                    │
│  ├── Risk: "We can't test that here—it might break things!"      │
│  ├── Observability: Limited visibility without affecting users   │
│  ├── Data privacy: Can't use real user data                       │
│  └── Rollback complexity: Hard to undo mistakes                   │
│                                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**The Cost of Environment Inconsistency**

When environments don't match, teams pay hidden costs that add up quickly:

- **Debugging time**: Engineers spend hours reproducing issues that only happen in specific environments
- **Delayed releases**: Confidence drops when tests pass locally but fail in staging
- **Production incidents**: The worst-case scenario—issues that only appear after deployment
- **Context switching**: Developers lose focus when pulled to investigate environment-specific failures
- **Tooling complexity**: Teams build workarounds instead of focusing on features

**What Teams Actually Need**

Through years of working with development teams, I've found that the ideal testing environment should be:

1. **Instant**: Available within minutes, not hours or days
2. **Isolated**: Your tests shouldn't affect anyone else's
3. **Identical**: Behaving exactly like production
4. **Ephemeral**: Disappearing when you're done, leaving no trace
5. **Scalable**: Able to handle anything from a simple API to a microservices mesh
6. **Cost-effective**: Using resources only when needed

This is exactly what Kubernetes provides.

content.title: How Kubernetes Solves These Challenges
content.explanation:
Kubernetes isn't just another tool—it's a fundamental shift in how we think about infrastructure. For API testing, it provides capabilities that were previously only available to large tech companies with massive engineering teams.

**The Kubernetes Solution: Ephemeral Environments**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    KUBERNETES TEST ENVIRONMENTS                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                   Kubernetes Cluster                       │  │
│  │  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐ │  │
│  │  │   PR #123    │    │   PR #124    │    │   PR #125    │ │  │
│  │  │  Environment │    │  Environment │    │  Environment │ │  │
│  │  │  ┌────────┐  │    │  ┌────────┐  │    │  ┌────────┐  │ │  │
│  │  │  │  API   │  │    │  │  API   │  │    │  │  API   │  │ │  │
│  │  │  │  Pod   │  │    │  │  Pod   │  │    │  │  Pod   │  │ │  │
│  │  │  └────────┘  │    │  └────────┘  │    │  └────────┘  │ │  │
│  │  │  ┌────────┐  │    │  ┌────────┐  │    │  ┌────────┐  │ │  │
│  │  │  │   DB   │  │    │  │   DB   │  │    │  │   DB   │  │ │  │
│  │  │  │  Pod   │  │    │  │  Pod   │  │    │  │  Pod   │  │ │  │
│  │  │  └────────┘  │    │  └────────┘  │    │  └────────┘  │ │  │
│  │  │  ┌────────┐  │    │  ┌────────┐  │    │  ┌────────┐  │ │  │
│  │  │  │ Redis  │  │    │  │ Redis  │  │    │  │ Redis  │  │ │  │
│  │  │  │  Pod   │  │    │  │  Pod   │  │    │  │  Pod   │  │ │  │
│  │  │  └────────┘  │    │  └────────┘  │    │  └────────┘  │ │  │
│  │  └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘ │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                   │
│  ✅ Each PR gets its own isolated environment                    │
│  ✅ Production-like configuration                                 │
│  ✅ Automatically created and destroyed                           │
│  ✅ Scales horizontally as teams grow                            │
│                                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Key Capabilities Kubernetes Provides**

| Capability | How Kubernetes Implements It | Testing Benefit |
|------------|------------------------------|-----------------|
| **Isolation** | Namespaces provide complete separation | Tests never interfere with each other |
| **Production Parity** | Same container images, same configs | High confidence before deployment |
| **Instant Environments** | API-driven resource creation | Environments in seconds, not hours |
| **Scalability** | Cluster can host hundreds of environments | Support growing teams without growing pain |
| **Resource Efficiency** | Share cluster, isolate workloads | Cost-effective at any scale |
| **Self-Service** | Developers create environments via CI/CD | No waiting, no tickets |
| **Reproducibility** | Declarative configuration | Same environment every time |

**Real-World Impact**

Teams that adopt Kubernetes for testing typically see dramatic improvements:

- **80% reduction** in environment-related test failures
- **90% faster** environment provisioning (from days to minutes)
- **Zero** environment contention—everyone gets their own
- **Production incidents** caused by environment mismatch nearly eliminated
- **Developer satisfaction** scores improve significantly—no more fighting environments

**Key Insight:** Kubernetes transforms testing from a constrained, shared resource into an abundant, on-demand capability. Each developer, each PR, each test run can have its own production-like environment, created in seconds and destroyed when done. This isn't just a nice-to-have—it's a competitive advantage that lets teams move faster with higher confidence.

content.title: Core Kubernetes Concepts for Testing
content.explanation:
Let's explore the Kubernetes building blocks you'll use most often when creating test environments. Think of these as your toolkit—each resource serves a specific purpose in the testing workflow.

**The Kubernetes Architecture (What Testers Need to Know)**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    KUBERNETES ARCHITECTURE                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │                    Kubernetes Cluster                    │    │
│  │                                                           │    │
│  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │    │
│  │  │                    Namespace                        │  │    │
│  │  │  ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐                │  │    │
│  │  │  │   Pod       │    │   Pod       │                │  │    │
│  │  │  │  ┌───────┐  │    │  ┌───────┐  │                │  │    │
│  │  │  │  │ API   │  │    │  │  DB   │  │                │  │    │
│  │  │  │  │Container│  │    │  │Container│  │                │  │    │
│  │  │  │  └───────┘  │    │  └───────┘  │                │  │    │
│  │  │  └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘                │  │    │
│  │  │                                                      │  │    │
│  │  │       Service ──────────┘                           │  │    │
│  │  │       (Stable network endpoint)                      │  │    │
│  │  │                                                      │  │    │
│  │  │       Ingress ──────────┐                           │  │    │
│  │  │       (External access)  │                           │  │    │
│  │  │                         ▼                           │  │    │
│  │  │                ┌─────────────────┐                  │  │    │
│  │  │                │   ConfigMap     │                  │  │    │
│  │  │                │  (Configuration) │                  │  │    │
│  │  │                └─────────────────┘                  │  │    │
│  │  │                ┌─────────────────┐                  │  │    │
│  │  │                │    Secret       │                  │  │    │
│  │  │                │  (Sensitive data)│                  │  │    │
│  │  │                └─────────────────┘                  │  │    │
│  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Key Resources Explained**

| Resource | What It Is | Testing Use Case | Real-World Analogy |
|----------|------------|------------------|-------------------|
| **Namespace** | A virtual cluster within the physical cluster | Isolate each PR's environment | A private office for each team |
| **Pod** | One or more containers that run together | Your API server, database, test runner | A single server rack |
| **Deployment** | Declares how to run and scale pods | Ensures your API keeps running | A manager ensuring workers are present |
| **Service** | Stable network endpoint to access pods | How your tests find the API | A reception desk with a fixed phone number |
| **Ingress** | External access with hostname/routing | Give each PR its own URL | The building's address and mailroom |
| **ConfigMap** | Non-sensitive configuration | Environment variables, feature flags | A whiteboard with settings |
| **Secret** | Sensitive configuration (base64 encoded) | API keys, database passwords | A locked safe |
| **Job** | Run-to-completion task | Execute test suite once | A temp worker with a specific task |
| **CronJob** | Scheduled task | Nightly regression tests | A scheduled cleaning service |

**A Complete Test Environment in YAML**

Let's see how these pieces fit together in a real test environment. This example creates an API deployment, a database, and a test runner—everything needed to validate a pull request.

```yaml
# First, create a namespace for isolation
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: test-pr-123  # Unique per PR
---
# Deploy the API under test
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: test-pr-123
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
      pr: "123"
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
        pr: "123"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: myapp/api:pr-123  # Built from PR code
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          value: postgres://user:pass@db-service:5432/testdb
        - name: API_KEY
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-secrets
              key: api-key
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
---
# Expose the API via a Service
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-service
  namespace: test-pr-123
spec:
  selector:
    app: api
    pr: "123"
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
---
# Deploy a database for this environment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: test-pr-123
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: testpass
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: testdb
---
# Run tests against this environment
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: test-runner
  namespace: test-pr-123
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: tests
        image: myapp/api-tests:latest
        env:
        - name: API_URL
          value: http://api-service  # Uses the Service
      restartPolicy: Never
```

**What This Gives You**

1. **Complete isolation**: Everything runs in its own namespace
2. **Production-like**: Same container images as production
3. **Self-contained**: Database, API, everything needed
4. **Testable**: Tests can access the API via the Service
5. **Cleanable**: Delete the namespace, everything goes away

**Key Insight:** You don't need to master every Kubernetes feature to use it effectively for testing. Focus on these core resources—they'll cover 90% of what you need. The beauty is that once you understand these building blocks, you can combine them in endless ways to create sophisticated test environments.

content.value:
The most important concept to internalize is the namespace. Think of it as your private sandbox—everything you create inside it is yours and yours alone. You can experiment freely, break things, and try again without affecting anyone else. When you're done, you delete the namespace, and everything inside disappears. This is the superpower that Kubernetes gives every developer and tester.

Once you're comfortable with these basics, you'll start to see patterns: every test environment is just a namespace with a collection of resources. Every PR can have its own namespace. Every test run can start with a fresh namespace and end by deleting it. This pattern scales from one developer to hundreds, and from a simple API to complex microservices architectures.

Ephemeral environments—environments that are created on demand and destroyed when no longer needed—are the killer feature of Kubernetes for testing. They solve the fundamental tension between isolation and resource efficiency. With traditional infrastructure, you had to choose: either give everyone their own environment (expensive and wasteful) or share environments (leading to contention and pollution). Kubernetes lets you have both: each user gets their own environment, but resources are only consumed while the environment exists.

Think of it like hotel rooms versus owning a home. A hotel room is created when you need it, perfectly suited to your needs, and cleaned up when you leave. You don't pay for it when you're not there, and you don't have to maintain it. Ephemeral test environments work the same way—they exist exactly as long as you need them, and no longer.

content.title: Namespace-per-PR Pattern
content.explanation:
The namespace-per-PR pattern is the foundation of ephemeral test environments. Every pull request gets its own namespace, its own copy of the API, its own database, and everything else needed to test the changes in isolation.

**The Pattern Explained**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    NAMESPACE-PER-PR FLOW                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                   │
│  1. PR Created                                                   │
│     │                                                            │
│     ▼                                                            │
│  2. Build container image from PR code                           │
│     │                                                            │
│     ▼                                                            │
│  3. Create namespace: pr-123                                     │
│     │                                                            │
│     ▼                                                            │
│  4. Deploy all components:                                       │
│     ├── API (using PR image)                                     │
│     ├── Database                                                  │
│     ├── Redis (if needed)                                        │
│     └── Any other dependencies                                   │
│     │                                                            │
│     ▼                                                            │
│  5. Run tests against this environment                           │
│     │                                                            │
│     ▼                                                            │
│  6. Report results back to PR                                    │
│     │                                                            │
│     ▼                                                            │
│  7. When PR is merged/closed: delete namespace                   │
│                                                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Complete Implementation**

Here's a real-world implementation of this pattern, with everything needed to automate the process:

```yaml
# pr-environment.yaml - Template with variables
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: pr-${PR_NUMBER}
---
# ConfigMap for non-sensitive configuration
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: api-config
  namespace: pr-${PR_NUMBER}
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: debug
  FEATURE_FLAGS: "new-api,beta-features"
  API_TIMEOUT: "30"
---
# Secrets (values would come from CI secrets)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: api-secrets
  namespace: pr-${PR_NUMBER}
type: Opaque
data:
  api-key: ${BASE64_ENCODED_API_KEY}
  jwt-secret: ${BASE64_ENCODED_JWT_SECRET}
---
# Database deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: pr-${PR_NUMBER}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
      pr: ${PR_NUMBER}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: postgres
        pr: ${PR_NUMBER}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: testpass
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: testdb
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: testuser
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
---
# Database service
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: pr-${PR_NUMBER}
spec:
  selector:
    app: postgres
    pr: ${PR_NUMBER}
  ports:
  - port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
---
# API deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: pr-${PR_NUMBER}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
      pr: ${PR_NUMBER}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
        pr: ${PR_NUMBER}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: myapp/api:pr-${PR_NUMBER}
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          value: postgresql://testuser:testpass@postgres:5432/testdb
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: api-config
              key: LOG_LEVEL
        - name: API_KEY
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-secrets
              key: api-key
        - name: JWT_SECRET
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-secrets
              key: jwt-secret
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
---
# API service
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: pr-${PR_NUMBER}
spec:
  selector:
    app: api
    pr: ${PR_NUMBER}
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
---
# Optional: Ingress for external access
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api-ingress
  namespace: pr-${PR_NUMBER}
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  rules:
  - host: pr-${PR_NUMBER}.test.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: api
            port:
              number: 80
```

**Automation Script**

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# deploy-pr-env.sh - Complete automation script

set -e  # Exit on any error

PR_NUMBER=$1
IMAGE_TAG=$2
API_KEY=$3
JWT_SECRET=$4

# Colors for output
RED='\033[0;31m'
GREEN='\033[0;32m'
YELLOW='\033[1;33m'
NC='\033[0m' # No Color

echo -e "${YELLOW}Creating environment for PR #$PR_NUMBER${NC}"

# Encode secrets for Kubernetes
API_KEY_B64=$(echo -n $API_KEY | base64)
JWT_SECRET_B64=$(echo -n $JWT_SECRET | base64)

# Process template and apply
cat pr-environment.yaml | \
  sed "s/\${PR_NUMBER}/$PR_NUMBER/g" | \
  sed "s/\${BASE64_ENCODED_API_KEY}/$API_KEY_B64/g" | \
  sed "s/\${BASE64_ENCODED_JWT_SECRET}/$JWT_SECRET_B64/g" | \
  kubectl apply -f -

# Wait for deployments to be ready
echo -e "${YELLOW}Waiting for API to be ready...${NC}"
kubectl rollout status deployment/api -n pr-$PR_NUMBER --timeout=120s

echo -e "${YELLOW}Waiting for database to be ready...${NC}"
kubectl rollout status deployment/postgres -n pr-$PR_NUMBER --timeout=60s

# Get the URL for this environment
if kubectl get ingress -n pr-$PR_NUMBER api-ingress &> /dev/null; then
  URL="http://pr-$PR_NUMBER.test.example.com"
else
  # Fallback to port-forward for local testing
  kubectl port-forward -n pr-$PR_NUMBER svc/api 8080:80 &
  PF_PID=$!
  sleep 3
  URL="http://localhost:8080"
fi

echo -e "${GREEN}Environment ready!${NC}"
echo -e "API URL: $URL"

# Run tests
echo -e "${YELLOW}Running tests...${NC}"

# Create test job
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: test-runner
  namespace: pr-$PR_NUMBER
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: tests
        image: myapp/api-tests:latest
        env:
        - name: API_URL
          value: http://api
        - name: TEST_SUITE
          value: "full"
        - name: API_KEY
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-secrets
              key: api-key
      restartPolicy: Never
  backoffLimit: 2
EOF

# Wait for test completion
echo -e "${YELLOW}Waiting for tests to complete...${NC}"
kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/test-runner -n pr-$PR_NUMBER --timeout=300s || {
  echo -e "${RED}Tests failed or timed out${NC}"
  kubectl logs job/test-runner -n pr-$PR_NUMBER
  exit 1
}

# Get test results
TEST_LOGS=$(kubectl logs job/test-runner -n pr-$PR_NUMBER)
echo -e "${GREEN}Test Results:${NC}"
echo "$TEST_LOGS"

# Kill port-forward if running
if [ ! -z "$PF_PID" ]; then
  kill $PF_PID 2>/dev/null || true
fi

echo -e "${GREEN}Environment pr-$PR_NUMBER is ready and tests passed!${NC}"
```

**GitHub Actions Integration**

```yaml
name: PR Environment

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, closed]

jobs:
  deploy:
    if: github.event.action != 'closed'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      
      - name: Configure kubectl
        uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
        with:
          kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
      
      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t myapp/api:pr-${{ github.event.number }} .
          docker push myapp/api:pr-${{ github.event.number }}
      
      - name: Deploy PR environment
        run: |
          chmod +x ./deploy-pr-env.sh
          ./deploy-pr-env.sh \
            ${{ github.event.number }} \
            pr-${{ github.event.number }} \
            "${{ secrets.API_KEY }}" \
            "${{ secrets.JWT_SECRET }}"
      
      - name: Comment PR with results
        uses: actions/github-script@v6
        with:
          script: |
            const url = `http://pr-${{ github.event.number }}.test.example.com`;
            github.rest.issues.createComment({
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              body: `## 🚀 PR Environment Deployed\n\n` +
                    `Your environment is ready at: ${url}\n\n` +
                    `✅ Tests passed!\n\n` +
                    `This environment will be automatically deleted when the PR is merged or closed.`
            });
  
  cleanup:
    if: github.event.action == 'closed'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Configure kubectl
        uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
        with:
          kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
      
      - name: Delete PR environment
        run: |
          kubectl delete namespace pr-${{ github.event.number }} --wait=false
          echo "Environment pr-${{ github.event.number }} deleted"
      
      - name: Comment on PR about cleanup
        uses: actions/github-script@v6
        with:
          script: |
            github.rest.issues.createComment({
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              body: `## 🧹 Environment Cleaned Up\n\n` +
                    `The test environment for this PR has been deleted.`
            });
```

**What Makes This Pattern Work**

1. **Naming convention**: `pr-123` makes it easy to identify environments
2. **Labels**: All resources are labeled with the PR number for easy selection
3. **Idempotency**: Running the script multiple times is safe (updates existing resources)
4. **Cleanup**: Namespace deletion removes everything atomically
5. **Visibility**: Ingress gives each PR its own URL for manual testing

**Key Insight**: The namespace-per-PR pattern turns infrastructure into a self-service resource. Developers don't need to ask for environments—they're created automatically. Testers don't need to coordinate—everyone has their own space. Ops doesn't need to clean up—it happens automatically. This is infrastructure that adapts to people, not the other way around.

content.value:
When I first implemented this pattern for a team of 50 developers, the impact was immediate and dramatic. Previously, we had two shared staging environments and a booking system where teams would reserve time slots. The wait could be days. With namespace-per-PR, every developer could have their own environment within minutes. The booking system was retired. The environment contention disputes disappeared. And perhaps most importantly, developers started testing more because it was easy—they didn't have to think about it.

The psychological shift was just as important as the technical one. When environments are scarce, testing becomes a gate—something to get through. When environments are abundant, testing becomes a tool—something that helps you build better software. Kubernetes makes abundance possible.

Databases are the most challenging part of ephemeral environments. Unlike stateless API servers that can be scaled and destroyed at will, databases contain state—and state is hard to make ephemeral. If every environment gets a fresh database, how do you populate it with realistic test data? If environments share a database, how do you prevent test pollution? These are the questions we'll answer in this section.

Think of it like setting up a test kitchen for a restaurant chain. You need ingredients that match what's used in the real restaurants, but you don't want to use the actual supply. You need to be able to experiment with new recipes without affecting the meals being served to customers. And when you're done, you need to clean up so the next chef can start fresh. Database strategies in Kubernetes follow the same logic.

content.title: Four Database Strategies Compared
content.explanation:
There's no one-size-fits-all solution for databases in ephemeral environments. The right choice depends on your data volume, schema complexity, and testing needs. Here are four proven strategies, with the trade-offs of each.

**Strategy 1: Fresh Database per Environment**

This is the simplest approach: each environment gets its own completely independent database instance.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: pr-$PR_NUMBER
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: testpass
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: testdb
        volumeMounts:
        - name: init-scripts
          mountPath: /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d
      volumes:
      - name: init-scripts
        configMap:
          name: db-init
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: db-init
  namespace: pr-$PR_NUMBER
data:
  01-schema.sql: |
    CREATE TABLE users (
        id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
        email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
        name VARCHAR(100),
        created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
    );
    
    CREATE TABLE orders (
        id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
        user_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id),
        total DECIMAL(10,2),
        status VARCHAR(50),
        created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
    );
  
  02-test-data.sql: |
    INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES
        ('test1@example.com', 'Test User 1'),
        ('test2@example.com', 'Test User 2');
    
    INSERT INTO orders (user_id, total, status) VALUES
        (1, 99.99, 'completed'),
        (1, 149.99, 'pending'),
        (2, 29.99, 'completed');
```

**Pros:**
- ✅ Complete isolation—tests cannot affect each other
- ✅ Fresh state every time—no pollution from previous runs
- ✅ Simple to understand and implement
- ✅ Easy to customize per environment

**Cons:**
- ❌ Resource intensive—each environment needs its own database
- ❌ Slower startup—databases take time to initialize
- ❌ Schema changes must be applied to all environments
- ❌ Test data must be regenerated each time

**Best For:** Teams with moderate environment counts (under 50 concurrent) and simple schemas where startup time isn't critical.

**Strategy 2: Database per Schema (Shared Instance)**

Instead of a separate database instance per environment, you run one database server and create a separate schema (or database) for each environment.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: test-services  # Single namespace for shared services
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: testpass
        - name: POSTGRES_MULTIPLE_DATABASES
          value: "pr-123,pr-124,pr-125"  # Comma-separated list
        volumeMounts:
        - name: init-script
          mountPath: /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sh
          subPath: init.sh
      volumes:
      - name: init-script
        configMap:
          name: db-init-script
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: db-init-script
data:
  init.sh: |
    #!/bin/bash
    set -e
    
    # Create databases for each environment
    for db in $(echo $POSTGRES_MULTIPLE_DATABASES | tr ',' ' '); do
      echo "Creating database: $db"
      psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 --username "$POSTGRES_USER" <<-EOSQL
        CREATE DATABASE $db;
EOSQL
    done
```

Each environment's API connects using a different database name:
```yaml
# In each environment's deployment
env:
- name: DATABASE_URL
  value: postgresql://postgres:testpass@postgres.test-services.svc.cluster.local:5432/pr-123
```

**Pros:**
- ✅ Resource efficient—one database server supports many environments
- ✅ Fast startup—no need to start new database pods
- ✅ Centralized management—schema updates in one place
- ✅ Lower overhead—fewer pods to manage

**Cons:**
- ❌ Less isolation—a problem in one schema could affect others
- ❌ Resource contention—environments compete for database resources
- ❌ Cleanup requires dropping schemas, not entire pods
- ❌ More complex connection management

**Best For:** Teams with many concurrent environments (50+) where resource efficiency is paramount and isolation requirements are moderate.

**Strategy 3: Database Snapshot + Clone**

Take a snapshot of a reference database (like a sanitized production copy) and clone it for each environment using storage snapshots.

```yaml
# Create a persistent volume claim for the reference data
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: postgres-reference
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadOnlyMany
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi
  storageClassName: fast-ssd
---
# Create a snapshot of the reference data
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshot
metadata:
  name: postgres-snapshot-$(date +%Y%m%d)
spec:
  volumeSnapshotClassName: csi-hostpath-snapclass
  source:
    persistentVolumeClaimName: postgres-reference
---
# For each environment, create a PVC from the snapshot
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: postgres-data-pr-123
  namespace: pr-123
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi
  dataSource:
    name: postgres-snapshot-20250225
    kind: VolumeSnapshot
    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
---
# Use the cloned volume in the database pod
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: pr-123
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: postgres-data-pr-123
```

**Pros:**
- ✅ Fast clones—snapshot-based cloning is nearly instantaneous
- ✅ Realistic data—use production-like data sets
- ✅ Consistent starting state—every environment starts from the same point
- ✅ Efficient storage—snapshots use copy-on-write, so they're space-efficient

**Cons:**
- ❌ Requires CSI snapshot support (not available on all clusters)
- ❌ More complex setup—requires storage configuration
- ❌ Data updates require new snapshots
- ❌ Can't modify the reference data without breaking clones

**Best For:** Teams with large, complex datasets where loading data from scratch is impractical. Perfect for performance testing with production-scale data.

**Strategy 4: Ephemeral Database with Init Container**

Use an init container to restore a database dump before the main database starts.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: pr-$PR_NUMBER
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: restore-dump
        image: postgres:15
        command:
          - sh
          - -c
          - |
            # Wait for database to start
            until pg_isready -h localhost -U postgres; do
              sleep 1
            done
            
            # Restore from dump
            pg_restore -U postgres -d testdb /dumps/base.dump
            
            # Apply any PR-specific migrations
            psql -U postgres -d testdb -f /migrations/${PR_NUMBER}.sql
        volumeMounts:
        - name: dumps
          mountPath: /dumps
        - name: migrations
          mountPath: /migrations
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
      
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: testpass
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: testdb
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
      
      volumes:
      - name: data
        emptyDir: {}  # Ephemeral storage
      - name: dumps
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: database-dumps
      - name: migrations
        configMap:
          name: pr-migrations
```

**Pros:**
- ✅ Fresh state every time
- ✅ Can use realistic data from dumps
- ✅ Can apply PR-specific migrations
- ✅ No shared resources—complete isolation

**Cons:**
- ❌ Slowest startup—restoring dumps takes time
- ❌ Requires maintaining database dumps
- ❌ Storage for dumps must be managed
- ❌ Complex init logic

**Best For:** Teams that need realistic data and complete isolation, and can tolerate longer startup times (e.g., for nightly test runs).

**Strategy Comparison Table**

| Strategy | Isolation | Startup Time | Resource Efficiency | Realistic Data | Complexity |
|----------|-----------|--------------|---------------------|----------------|------------|
| Fresh DB | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | Slow | Low | Synthetic | Low |
| Schema per Env | ⭐⭐⭐ | Instant | High | Synthetic | Medium |
| Snapshot Clone | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ | Fast | Medium | Production-like | High |
| Init Restore | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | Slow | Medium | Production-like | High |

**Choosing the Right Strategy**

Here's a decision flowchart to help you choose:

```
Start: How many concurrent environments?
           |
           ▼
    < 50 ──────────────> 50+
      |                     |
      ▼                     ▼
Need realistic data?   Use Schema per Env
      |                     |
   ┌──┴──┐                  |
   ▼     ▼                  |
  Yes    No                 |
   |     |                  |
   ▼     ▼                  |
Snapshot  Fresh DB          |
  or       |                |
  Init     |                |
   |       |                |
   └───┬───┘                |
       |                    |
       ▼                    |
  Need fast startup?        |
       |                    |
   ┌───┴───┐                |
   ▼       ▼                |
  Yes      No               |
   |       |                |
   ▼       ▼                |
Snapshot  Init              |
   |       |                |
   └───┬───┘                |
       |                    |
       └────────────────────┘
                    |
                    ▼
           Implement chosen strategy
```

**Key Insight:** There's no perfect database strategy—each makes trade-offs between isolation, speed, efficiency, and realism. Start with the simplest approach that meets your needs (likely fresh databases), and evolve as you scale. The right strategy today might not be right next year, and that's okay. Kubernetes gives you the flexibility to change strategies as your needs evolve.

content.value:
I've seen teams get paralyzed trying to choose the "perfect" database strategy. Don't fall into this trap. Start with fresh databases—they're simple, they work, and they'll teach you what you need to know. As your team grows, you'll discover the limitations of your current approach organically. Maybe startup time becomes an issue, so you move to schema-per-environment. Maybe data realism becomes critical, so you implement snapshots. Each step teaches you something about your actual needs.

The beauty of Kubernetes is that these strategies aren't mutually exclusive. You can use fresh databases for small PRs, snapshots for performance testing, and schema-per-environment for your main development branch. The platform gives you the flexibility to use the right tool for each job.

As you create more test environments, you'll quickly tire of writing the same YAML over and over. You'll also discover that your production YAML and your test YAML are mostly the same—just with different replica counts, resource limits, and configurations. This is where Helm comes in.

Think of Helm as a package manager for Kubernetes, like apt for Ubuntu or brew for macOS. But more importantly, it's a templating engine that lets you define your infrastructure once and reuse it everywhere. Your test environments become parameterized templates—change a few values, and you get a completely different environment.

content.title: Packaging Test Environments with Helm
content.explanation:
Helm charts transform your raw YAML into reusable, configurable templates. Instead of copying and pasting YAML for each environment, you define it once and customize with values.

**Helm Chart Structure**

```
helm-charts/
├── api-test-env/
│   ├── Chart.yaml          # Metadata (name, version, description)
│   ├── values.yaml         # Default configuration values
│   ├── values-pr.yaml      # PR-specific values
│   ├── values-staging.yaml # Staging-specific values
│   └── templates/          # Template files
│       ├── _helpers.tpl    # Helper templates (reusable snippets)
│       ├── namespace.yaml
│       ├── deployment-api.yaml
│       ├── deployment-db.yaml
│       ├── service.yaml
│       ├── ingress.yaml
│       ├── configmap.yaml
│       ├── secrets.yaml
│       └── test-job.yaml
```

**Chart.yaml - The Metadata**

```yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: api-test-env
description: A Helm chart for API test environments
type: application
version: 0.1.0
appVersion: "1.0.0"

# Dependencies (if your environment needs other charts)
dependencies:
  - name: postgres
    version: 12.1.0
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: postgres.enabled
  - name: redis
    version: 17.3.0
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: redis.enabled
```

**values.yaml - Default Configuration**

```yaml
# Default values for api-test-env
# This is a YAML-formatted file.
# Declare variables to be passed into your templates.

# Namespace configuration
namespace:
  name: test-env  # Will be overridden per environment
  create: true

# Image configuration
image:
  repository: myapp/api
  tag: latest
  pullPolicy: Always

# API service configuration
api:
  name: api
  replicas: 1
  port: 3000
  service:
    type: ClusterIP
    port: 80
  resources:
    requests:
      memory: 256Mi
      cpu: 250m
    limits:
      memory: 512Mi
      cpu: 500m
  env:
    LOG_LEVEL: info
    FEATURE_FLAG_A: "false"
    FEATURE_FLAG_B: "false"
  probes:
    liveness:
      enabled: true
      path: /health
      initialDelaySeconds: 30
      periodSeconds: 10
    readiness:
      enabled: true
      path: /ready
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 5

# Database configuration
database:
  enabled: true
  image: postgres:15
  password: testpass
  database: testdb
  resources:
    requests:
      memory: 256Mi
      cpu: 250m
    limits:
      memory: 512Mi
      cpu: 500m
  persistence:
    enabled: false  # Ephemeral by default
    size: 10Gi
  initScripts:
    enabled: true
    schema: |
      CREATE TABLE users (
          id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
          email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
          name VARCHAR(100),
          created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
      );
    testData: |
      INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES
          ('test1@example.com', 'Test User 1'),
          ('test2@example.com', 'Test User 2');

# Redis configuration
redis:
  enabled: false
  image: redis:7-alpine
  resources:
    requests:
      memory: 128Mi
      cpu: 100m
    limits:
      memory: 256Mi
      cpu: 200m

# Ingress configuration
ingress:
  enabled: true
  host: test-env.example.com
  tls: false
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx

# Test runner configuration
tests:
  image: myapp/api-tests:latest
  suite: regression
  timeout: 300
  resources:
    requests:
      memory: 256Mi
      cpu: 250m
    limits:
      memory: 512Mi
      cpu: 500m
```

**templates/_helpers.tpl - Reusable Snippets**

```yaml
{{- define "api-test-env.name" -}}
{{- default .Chart.Name .Values.nameOverride | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }}
{{- end }}

{{- define "api-test-env.fullname" -}}
{{- if .Values.fullnameOverride }}
{{- .Values.fullnameOverride | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }}
{{- else }}
{{- $name := default .Chart.Name .Values.nameOverride }}
{{- if contains $name .Release.Name }}
{{- .Release.Name | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }}
{{- else }}
{{- printf "%s-%s" .Release.Name $name | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }}
{{- end }}
{{- end }}
{{- end }}

{{- define "api-test-env.labels" -}}
helm.sh/chart: {{ include "api-test-env.name" . }}-{{ .Chart.Version | replace "+" "_" }}
{{ include "api-test-env.selectorLabels" . }}
{{- if .Chart.AppVersion }}
app.kubernetes.io/version: {{ .Chart.AppVersion | quote }}
{{- end }}
app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: {{ .Release.Service }}
{{- end }}

{{- define "api-test-env.selectorLabels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ include "api-test-env.name" . }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end }}

{{- define "api-test-env.databaseUrl" -}}
{{- if .Values.database.enabled }}
postgresql://postgres:{{ .Values.database.password }}@{{ .Release.Name }}-postgres:5432/{{ .Values.database.database }}
{{- else }}
{{- .Values.database.externalUrl | default "" }}
{{- end }}
{{- end }}
```

**templates/deployment-api.yaml**

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Values.api.name | default "api" }}
  namespace: {{ .Values.namespace.name }}
  labels:
    {{- include "api-test-env.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
    component: api
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.api.replicas }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "api-test-env.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }}
      component: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        {{- include "api-test-env.selectorLabels" . | nindent 8 }}
        component: api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
        imagePullPolicy: {{ .Values.image.pullPolicy }}
        ports:
        - containerPort: {{ .Values.api.port }}
          name: http
        env:
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          value: {{ include "api-test-env.databaseUrl" . }}
        - name: PORT
          value: "{{ .Values.api.port }}"
        {{- range $key, $value := .Values.api.env }}
        - name: {{ $key }}
          value: "{{ $value }}"
        {{- end }}
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: {{ .Release.Name }}-config
        {{- if .Values.database.enabled }}
        - secretRef:
            name: {{ .Release.Name }}-secrets
        {{- end }}
        resources:
          {{- toYaml .Values.api.resources | nindent 10 }}
        {{- if .Values.api.probes.liveness.enabled }}
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: {{ .Values.api.probes.liveness.path }}
            port: {{ .Values.api.port }}
          initialDelaySeconds: {{ .Values.api.probes.liveness.initialDelaySeconds }}
          periodSeconds: {{ .Values.api.probes.liveness.periodSeconds }}
        {{- end }}
        {{- if .Values.api.probes.readiness.enabled }}
```
